description: We're a team of young women from Uruguay united by our passion for science, technology, and space exploration. We met through Mission ShakthiSAT as finalists and later welcomed  a new member joined us for Space Challenge. Inspired by the Seven Sisters star cluster, we chose the name The Pleiades, symbolizing unity through diversity. We are driven by creativity, initiative, and resourcefulness, we aim to turn our ideas and knowledge into innovative contributions to the future of space exploration
summary:
Hypatia is a multilingual web application designed to identify, compare, and locate terrestrial environments that replicate specific conditions found on other celestial bodies, particularly Mars and the Moon.

Rather than focusing solely on visual similarities, our platform analyzes environmental and geographical variables, such as temperature, geology, mineralogy, terrain, radiation, and illumination, to identify potential locations for scientific research, experiments, and space mission simulations.

Through customizable search filters, an interactive map, and an AI-powered assistant, users can explore locations that match their research requirements. The system combines publicly available NASA scientific resources with independent research conducted by our team, allowing us to identify promising analog environments beyond those already officially recognized or studied.

Available in English, Spanish, and Italian, Hypatia aims to make the search for terrestrial analog sites more accessible to researchers, universities, students, and space exploration teams worldwide.

By transforming accessible scientific data into a practical research tool, we hope to expand opportunities for experimentation on Earth and contribute to preparing humanity for future exploration of other worlds.
details:
HYPATIA: Habitat Yielding Planetary Analogue Terrain Identification and Assessment.

What if we could find on Earth the conditions needed to prepare ourselves for exploring other planets?

This question inspired Hypatia, our proposal for Space Challenge, as part of the Space Analog Facilities Search Project: Global Directory of Terrestrial Space Analog Habitats challenge.

Our proposal consists of developing a web application that allows users to identify, compare, and locate terrestrial environments with characteristics similar to those found on other celestial bodies, such as Mars or the Moon. Our goal is to facilitate the search for locations where research, simulations, and tests related to future space missions can be conducted.

We designed the platform with an international perspective, which is why it will be available in three languages: Spanish, English, and Italian, allowing people from different parts of the world to access its tools and content.

However, our proposal goes beyond simply finding landscapes that visually resemble other planets. We understand that, for scientific research, what truly matters are the conditions present in each environment.

For example, if a research team needs to test how a piece of technological equipment would perform under certain temperature conditions similar to those it might experience on Mars, our application allows users to search for terrestrial regions with comparable thermal conditions. The same applies to other environmental and geographical variables. We are not simply looking for a place that looks like Mars, but rather one that meets the specific characteristics researchers need to study or simulate.

To achieve this, we developed a search system with customizable filters, allowing users to select the conditions they wish to investigate. Based on these criteria, the application identifies potential locations, displays them on an interactive map, and provides different alternatives according to how closely they match the selected characteristics. 

In addition, we incorporated artificial intelligence to assist users throughout this process. We integrated an AI system that uses scientific information from NASA, along with data collected for the project, to guide searches, analyze selected criteria, and help identify the locations that best meet the needs of each research project.

One of the aspects we are particularly interested in highlighting is that we do not limit ourselves to including locations that have already been identified or studied by NASA as potential space analog sites. We also conduct our own research and select places that have not necessarily been explored by NASA or officially recognized as analog environments, but which we consider promising for future testing and simulations due to their environmental and geographical characteristics by using software trained on NASA's public database and the provided resources.

In this way, we aim to expand research opportunities by introducing new locations that may be of interest to the scientific community. We do not want to limit ourselves to presenting what is already known; we also want to explore new possibilities through research and the analysis of our planet's characteristics.

Another important aspect of our proposal is the combination of different information sources. We incorporate official NASA resources and scientific data, which we complement with our own recommendations, locations, and research. This means that we do not simply collect existing information; we also contribute our own research and selection process.

We are also committed to making the most of the resources available to us. We use publicly accessible scientific information, digital tools, and artificial intelligence to transform data and knowledge into a technological solution with international potential, without relying on large-scale infrastructure or substantial budgets. We believe that innovation also means knowing how to creatively use what we have at our disposal and finding new ways to make the most of existing resources.

We believe this tool could be useful for researchers, universities, students, scientific institutions, and teams involved in space exploration, as it helps streamline the identification of suitable terrestrial environments for conducting tests and simulations before carrying out research on other worlds.

The name we chose for our application is Hypatia, inspired by Hypatia of Alexandria, an ancient mathematician, philosopher, and astronomer. Her legacy represents curiosity, scientific thinking, and the pursuit of knowledge. We see a connection between her legacy and our identity as a team of young women interested in science and technology. We want our project to reflect those same values: questioning, researching, and discovering new possibilities.

Our goal is to build an accessible, interactive, and global platform that connects Earth's geography with space research, making it easier to discover locations that can become true natural laboratories.

Because preparing ourselves to explore other worlds may not begin with traveling into space, but rather with learning to discover everything our own planet still has to offer.
